entries.18cdef2e63b4a7d574a3b7dd665e97f27b3a79cf: <div sID="gen16160" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="32" osisID="Isa.32" sID="Isa.32"/> <div eID="gen16160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16161" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16162" type="x-p"/> This chapter seems to be such a prophecy of the reign of Hezekiah as amounts to an abridgment of the history of it, and this with an eye to the kingdom of the Messiah, whose government was typified by the thrones of the house of David, for which reason he is so often called "the Son of David." Here is, I. A prophecy of that good work of reformation with which he should begin his reign, and the happy influence it should have upon the people, who had been wretchedly corrupted and debauched in the reign of his predecessor, <reference osisRef="Isa.32.1-Isa.32.8">ver. 1-8</reference>. II. A prophecy of the great disturbance that would be given to the kingdom in the middle of his reign by the Assyrian invasion, <reference osisRef="Isa.32.9-Isa.32.14">ver. 9-14</reference>. III. A promise of better times afterwards, towards the latter end of his reign, in respect both of piety and peace (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.15-Isa.32.20">ver. 15-20</reference>), which promise may be supposed to look as far forward as the days of the Messiah.
entries.7265b892b7870acedbbb28f6a3bf10f953b43607: <div eID="gen16162" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16161" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Reign of Justice. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 726.)</title> <div sID="gen16163" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Behold, a king shall reign in righteousness, and princes shall rule in judgment. <hi type="super">2</hi> And a man shall be as a hiding place from the wind, and a covert from the tempest; as rivers of water in a dry place, as the shadow of a great rock in a weary land. <hi type="super">3</hi> And the eyes of them that see shall not be dim, and the ears of them that hear shall hearken. <hi type="super">4</hi> The heart also of the rash shall understand knowledge, and the tongue of the stammerers shall be ready to speak plainly. <hi type="super">5</hi> The vile person shall be no more called liberal, nor the churl said <hi type="italic">to be</hi> bountiful. <hi type="super">6</hi> For the vile person will speak villany, and his heart will work iniquity, to practise hypocrisy, and to utter error against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , to make empty the soul of the hungry, and he will cause the drink of the thirsty to fail. <hi type="super">7</hi> The instruments also of the churl <hi type="italic">are</hi> evil: he deviseth wicked devices to destroy the poor with lying words, even when the needy speaketh right. <hi type="super">8</hi> But the liberal deviseth liberal things; and by liberal things shall he stand. <div eID="gen16163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16164" type="x-p"/> We have here the description of a flourishing kingdom. "<hi type="italic">Blessed art thou, O land!</hi> when it is thus with thee, when kings, princes, and people, are in their places such as they should be." It may be taken as a directory both to magistrates and subjects, what both ought to do, or as a panegyric to Hezekiah, who ruled well and saw something of the happy effects of his good government, and it was designed to make the people sensible how happy they were under his administration and how careful they should be to improve the advantages of it, and withal to direct them to look for the kingdom of Christ, and the times of reformation which that kingdom should introduce. It is here promised and prescribed, for the comfort of the church, <div eID="gen16164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16165" type="x-p"/> I. That magistrates should do their duty in their places, and the powers answer the great ends for which they were ordained of God, <reference osisRef="Isa.32.1-Isa.32.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. 1. There shall be a king and princes that shall reign and rule; for it cannot go well when there is no king in Israel. The princes must have a king, a monarch over them as supreme, in whom they may unite; and the king must have princes under him as officers, by whom he may act, <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.13-1Pet.2.14">1 Pet. ii. 13, 14</reference>. They both shall know their place and fill it up. The king shall reign, and yet, without any diminution to his just prerogative, the princes shall rule in a lower sphere, and all for the public good. 2. They shall use their power according to law, and not against it. They shall reign in righteousness and in judgment, with wisdom and equity, protecting the good and punishing the bad; and those kings and princes Christ owns as reigning by him who decree justice, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.15">Prov. viii. 15</reference>. Such a King, such a Prince, Christ himself is; he reigns by rule, and <hi type="italic">in righteousness will he judge the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.9.7">ch. ix. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.11.4">xi. 4</reference>. 3. Thus they shall be great blessings to the people (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">A man,</hi> that man, that king that reigns in righteousness, <hi type="italic">shall be as a hiding-place.</hi> When princes are as they should be people are as they would be. (1.) They are sheltered and protected from many mischiefs. This good magistrate is a covert to the subject from the tempest of injury and violence; he <hi type="italic">defends the poor and fatherless,</hi> that they be not made a prey of by the mighty. Whither should oppressed innocency flee, when blasted by reproach or borne down by violence, but to the magistrate as its hiding-place? To him it appeals, and by him it is righted. (2.) They are refreshed and comforted with many blessings. This good magistrate gives such countenance to those that are poor and in distress, and such encouragement to every thing that is praiseworthy, that he is <hi type="italic">as rivers of water in a dry place,</hi> cooling and cherishing the earth and making it fruitful, and <hi type="italic">as the shadow of a great rock,</hi> under which a poor traveller may shelter himself from the scorching heat of the sun <hi type="italic">in a weary land.</hi> It is a great reviving to a good man, who makes conscience of doing his duty, in the midst of contempt and contradiction, at length to be backed, and favoured, and smiled upon in it by a good magistrate. All this, and much more, the man Christ Jesus is to all the willing faithful subjects of his kingdom. When the greatest evils befal us, not only the wind, but the tempest, when storms of guilt and wrath beset us and beat upon us, they drive us to Christ, and in him we are not only safe, but satisfied that we are so; in him we find rivers of water for those that hunger and thirst after righteousness, all the refreshment and comfort that a needy soul can desire, and the shadow, not of a tree, which sun or rain may beat through, but of a rock, of a great rock, which reaches a great way for the shelter of the traveller. Some observe here that as the covert, and the hiding-place, and the rock, do themselves receive the battering of the wind and storm, to save those from it that take shelter in them, so Christ bore the storm himself to keep it off from us. <div eID="gen16165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16166" type="x-p"/> II. That subjects should do their duty in their places. <div eID="gen16166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16167" type="x-p"/> 1. They shall be willing to be taught, and to understand things aright. They shall lay aside their prejudices against their rulers and teachers, and submit to the light and power of truth, <reference osisRef="Isa.32.3">v. 3</reference>. When this blessed work of reformation is set on foot, and men do their parts towards it, God will not be wanting to do his: Then <hi type="italic">the eyes of those that see,</hi> of the prophets, the seers, <hi type="italic">shall not be dim;</hi> but God will bless them with visions, to be by them communicated to the people; and those that read the word written shall no longer have a veil upon their hearts, but shall see things clearly. Then <hi type="italic">the ears of those that hear</hi> the word preached <hi type="italic">shall hearken</hi> diligently and readily receive what they hear, and not be so dull of hearing as they have been. This shall be done by the grace of God, especially gospel-grace; for <hi type="italic">the hearing ear, and the seeing eyes, the Lord has made,</hi> has new-made, even both of them. <div eID="gen16167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16168" type="x-p"/> 2. There shall be a wonderful change wrought in them by that which is taught them, <reference osisRef="Isa.32.4">v. 4</reference>. (1.) They shall have a clear head, and be able to discern things that differ, and distinguish concerning them. <hi type="italic">The heart of those that were</hi> hasty and <hi type="italic">rash,</hi> and could not take time to digest and consider things, shall now be cured of their precipitation, and <hi type="italic">shall understand knowledge;</hi> for the Spirit of God will open their understanding. This blessed work Christ wrought in his disciples after his resurrection (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.45">Luke xxiv. 45</reference>), as a specimen of what he would do for all his people, in giving them an understanding, <reference osisRef="1John.5.20">1 John v. 20</reference>. The pious designs of good princes are likely to take effect when their subjects allow themselves liberty to consider, and to think, so freely as to take things right. (2.) They shall have a ready utterance: <hi type="italic">The tongue of the stammerers,</hi> that used to blunder whenever they spoke of the things of God, <hi type="italic">shall</hi> now <hi type="italic">be ready to speak plainly,</hi> as those that understand what they speak of, that believe, and therefore speak. There shall be a great increase of such clear, distinct, and methodical knowledge in the things of God, that those from whom one would not have expected it shall speak intelligently of these things, very much to the honour of God and the edification of others. Their hearts being full of this good matter, their tongues shall be <hi type="italic">as the pen of a ready writer,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.45.1">Ps. xlv. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen16168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16169" type="x-p"/> 3. The differences between good and evil, virtue and vice, shall be kept up, and no more confounded by those who put darkness for light and light for darkness (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">The vile shall no more be called liberal.</hi> <div eID="gen16169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16170" type="x-p"/> (1.) Bad men shall no more be preferred by the prince. When a king reigns in justice he will not put those in places of honour and power that are ill-natured, and of base and sordid spirits, and care not what injury or mischief they do so they may but compass their own ends. Such as <hi type="italic">vile</hi> persons (as Antiochus is called, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.21">Dan. xi. 21</reference>); when they are advanced they are called <hi type="italic">liberal</hi> and <hi type="italic">bountiful;</hi> they are called <hi type="italic">benefactors</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.25">Luke xxii. 25</reference>): but it shall not always be thus; when the world grows wiser men shall be preferred according to their merit, and honour (which was never thought seemly for a fool, <reference osisRef="Prov.26.1">Prov. xxvi. 1</reference>) shall no longer be thrown away upon such. <div eID="gen16170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16171" type="x-p"/> (2.) Bad men shall be no more had in reputation among the people, nor vice disguised with the colours of virtue. It shall no more be said to Nabal, <hi type="italic">Thou art Nadib</hi> (so the words are); such a covetous muck-worm as Nabal was, a fool but for his money, shall not be complimented with the title of a gentleman or a prince; nor shall they call a <hi type="italic">churl,</hi> that minds none but himself, does no good with what he has, but is an unprofitable burden of the earth, <hi type="italic">My lord;</hi> or, rather, they shall not say of him, <hi type="italic">He is rich;</hi> for so the word signifies. Those only are to be reckoned rich that are rich in good works; not those that have abundance, but those that use it well. In short, it is well with a people when men are generally valued by their virtue, and usefulness, and beneficence to mankind, and not by their wealth or titles of honour. Whether this was fulfilled in the reign of Hezekiah, and how far it refers to the kingdom of Christ (in which we are sure men are judged of by what they are, not by what they have, nor is any man's character mistaken), we will not say; but it prescribes an excellent rule both to prince and people, to respect men according to their personal merit. To enforce this rule, here is a description both of the vile person and of the liberal; and by it we shall see such a vast difference between them that we must quite forget ourselves if we pay that respect to the vile person and the churl which is due only to the liberal. <div eID="gen16171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16172" type="x-p"/> [1.] A vile person and a churl will do mischief, and the more if he be preferred and have power in his hand; his honours will make him worse and not better, <reference osisRef="Isa.32.6-Isa.32.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. See the character of these base ill-conditioned men. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> They are always plotting some unjust thing or other, designing ill either to particular persons or to the public, and contriving how to bring it about; and so many silly piques they have to gratify, and mean revenges, that there appears not in them the least spark of generosity. Their hearts will be still working some iniquity or other. Observe, There is the work of the heart, as well as the work of the hands. As thoughts are words to God, so designs are works in his account. See what pains sinners take in sin. They labour at it; their hearts are intent upon it, and with a great deal of art and application they <hi type="italic">work iniquity.</hi> They <hi type="italic">devise wicked devices</hi> with all the subtlety of the old serpent and a great deal of deliberation, which makes the sin exceedingly sinful; and the more there is of plot and management in a sin the more there is of Satan in it. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They carry on their plots by trick and dissimulation. When they are meditating iniquity, they <hi type="italic">practise hypocrisy,</hi> feign themselves just men, <reference osisRef="Luke.20.20">Luke xx. 20</reference>. The most abominable mischiefs shall be disguised with the most plausible pretences of devotion to God, regard to man, and concern for some common good. Those are the vilest of men that intend the worst mischiefs when they speak fair. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> They <hi type="italic">speak villainy.</hi> When they are in a passion you will see what they are by the base ill language they give to those about them, which no way becomes men of rank and honour; or, in giving verdict or judgment, they villainously put false colours upon things, to pervert justice. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> They affront God, who is a righteous God and loves righteousness: They <hi type="italic">utter error against the Lord,</hi> and therein they practise profaneness; for so the word which we translate <hi type="italic">hypocrisy</hi> signifies. They give an unjust sentence, and then profanely make use of the name of God for the ratification of it; as if, because the <hi type="italic">judgment is God's</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.17">Deut. i. 17</reference>), therefore their false and unjust judgment was his. This is <hi type="italic">uttering error against the Lord,</hi> under pretence of uttering truth and justice for him; and nothing can be more impudently done against God than to use his name to patronise wickedness. <hi type="italic">Fifthly,</hi> They abuse mankind, those particularly whom they are bound to protect and relieve. 1. Instead of supplying the wants of the poor, they impoverish them, they <hi type="italic">make empty the souls of the hungry;</hi> either taking away the food they have, or, which is almost equivalent, denying the supply which they want and which they have to give. And they <hi type="italic">cause the drink of the thirsty to fail;</hi> they cut off the relief they used to have, though they need it as much as ever. Those are vile persons indeed that rob the spital. 2. Instead of righting the poor, when they appeal to their judgment, they contrive to destroy the poor, to ruin them in their courts of judicature with lying words in favour of the rich, to whom they are plainly partial; yea, though the needy speak right, though the evidence be ever so full for them to make out the equity of their cause, it is the bribe that governs them, not the right. <hi type="italic">Sixthly,</hi> These churls and vile persons have always had instruments about them, that are ready to serve their villainous purposes: <hi type="italic">All their servants are wicked.</hi> There is no design so palpably unjust but there may be found those that would be employed as tools to put it in execution. <hi type="italic">The instruments of the churl are evil,</hi> and one cannot expect otherwise; but this is our comfort, that they can do no more mischief than God permits them. <div eID="gen16172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16173" type="x-p"/> [2.] One that is truly liberal, and deserves the honour of being called so, makes it his business to do good to every body according as his sphere is, <reference osisRef="Isa.32.8">v. 8</reference>. Observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The care he takes, and the contrivances he has, to do good. He <hi type="italic">devises liberal things.</hi> As much as the churl or niggard projects how to save and lay up what he has for himself only, so much the good charitable man projects how to use and lay out what he has in the best manner for the good of others. Charity must be directed by wisdom, and liberal things done prudently and with device, that the good intention of them may be answered, that it may not be charity misplaced. The liberal man, when he has done all the liberal things that are in his own power, devises liberal things for others to do according to their power, and puts them upon doing them. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> the comfort he takes, and the advantage he has, in doing good: <hi type="italic">By liberal things he shall stand,</hi> or be established. The providence of God will reward him for his liberality with a settled prosperity and an established reputation. The grace of God will give him abundance of satisfaction and confirmed peace in his own bosom. What disquiets others shall not disturb him; his heart is fixed. This is the recompence of charity, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.5-Ps.112.6">Ps. cxii. 5, 6</reference>. Some read it, <hi type="italic">The prince, or honourable man, will take honourable courses; and by such honourable or ingenuous courses he shall stand or be established.</hi> It is well with a land when the honourable of it are indeed men of honour and scorn to do a base thing, when its king is thus the son of nobles.
entries.18191dd52c7fa5b7648ec71fa2cdaf9a2d5341ea: <div eID="gen16173" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Joyful Prospects. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 726.)</title> <div sID="gen16174" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> Rise up, ye women that are at ease; hear my voice, ye careless daughters; give ear unto my speech. <hi type="super">10</hi> Many days and years shall ye be troubled, ye careless women: for the vintage shall fail, the gathering shall not come. <hi type="super">11</hi> Tremble, ye women that are at ease; be troubled, ye careless ones: strip you, and make you bare, and gird <hi type="italic">sackcloth</hi> upon <hi type="italic">your</hi> loins. <hi type="super">12</hi> They shall lament for the teats, for the pleasant fields, for the fruitful vine. <hi type="super">13</hi> Upon the land of my people shall come up thorns <hi type="italic">and</hi> briers; yea, upon all the houses of joy <hi type="italic">in</hi> the joyous city: <hi type="super">14</hi> Because the palaces shall be forsaken; the multitude of the city shall be left; the forts and towers shall be for dens for ever, a joy of wild asses, a pasture of flocks; <hi type="super">15</hi> Until the spirit be poured upon us from on high, and the wilderness be a fruitful field, and the fruitful field be counted for a forest. <hi type="super">16</hi> Then judgment shall dwell in the wilderness, and righteousness remain in the fruitful field. <hi type="super">17</hi> And the work of righteousness shall be peace; and the effect of righteousness quietness and assurance for ever. <hi type="super">18</hi> And my people shall dwell in a peaceable habitation, and in sure dwellings, and in quiet resting places; <hi type="super">19</hi> When it shall hail, coming down on the forest; and the city shall be low in a low place. <hi type="super">20</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">are</hi> ye that sow beside all waters, that send forth <hi type="italic">thither</hi> the feet of the ox and the ass. <div eID="gen16174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16175" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have God rising up to judgment against the vile persons, to punish them for their villainy; but at length returning in mercy to the liberal, to reward them for their liberality. <div eID="gen16175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16176" type="x-p"/> I. When there was so great a corruption of manners, and so much provocation given to the holy God, bad times might well be expected, and here is a warning given of such times coming. The alarm is sounded to the <hi type="italic">women that were at ease</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.9">v. 9</reference>) and the <hi type="italic">careless daughters,</hi> to feed whose pride, vanity, and luxury, their husbands and fathers were tempted to starve the poor. Let them hear what the prophet has to say to them in God's name: "<hi type="italic">Rise up, and hear</hi> with reverence and attention." <div eID="gen16176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16177" type="x-p"/> 1. Let them know that God was about to bring wasting desolating judgments upon the land in which they <hi type="italic">lived in pleasure and were wanton.</hi> This seems to refer primarily to the desolations made by Sennacherib's army when he seized all the fenced cities of Judah: but then those words, <hi type="italic">many days and years,</hi> must be rendered (as the margin reads them) <hi type="italic">days above a year,</hi> that is, something above a year shall this havock be in the making: so long it was from the first entrance of that army into the land of Judah to the overthrow of it. But it is applicable to the wretched disappointment which those will certainly meet with, first or last, that set their hearts upon the world and place their happiness in it: <hi type="italic">You shall be troubled, you careless women.</hi> It will not secure us from trouble to cast away care when we are at ease; nay, to those who affect to live carelessly even little troubles will be great vexations and press hard upon them. They were careless and at ease because they had money enough and mirth enough; but the prophet here tells them, (1.) That the country whence they had their tents and dainties should shortly be laid waste: "<hi type="italic">The vintage shall fail;</hi> and then what will you do for wine to make merry with? <hi type="italic">The gathering</hi> of fruit <hi type="italic">shall not come,</hi> for there shall be none to be gathered, and you will find the want of them, <reference osisRef="Isa.32.10">v. 10</reference>. You will want <hi type="italic">the teats,</hi> the good milk from the cows, <hi type="italic">the pleasant fields</hi> and their productions:" the useful fields that are serviceable to human life are the pleasant ones. "You will want the fruitful vine, and the grapes it used to yield you." The abuse of plenty is justly punished with scarcity; and those deserve to be deprived of the supports of life who make them the food and fuel of lust and prepare them for Baal. (2.) That the cities too, the cities of Judah, where they lived at ease, spent their rents, and made themselves merry with their dainties, should be laid waste (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.13-Isa.32.14">v. 13, 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">Briers and thorns,</hi> the fruits of sin and the curse, <hi type="italic">shall come up,</hi> not only <hi type="italic">upon the land of my people,</hi> which shall lie uncultivated, but upon <hi type="italic">all the houses of joy</hi>—the play-houses, the gaming-houses, the taverns—<hi type="italic">in the joyous cities.</hi> When a foreign army was ravaging the country the houses of joy, no doubt, became houses of mourning; then the palaces, or noblemen's houses, were forsaken by their owners, who perhaps fled to Egypt for refuge; the multitude of the city were left by their leaders to shift for themselves. Then the stately houses <hi type="italic">shall be for dens for ever,</hi> which had been as forts and towers for strength and magnificence. They shall be abandoned; the owners shall never return to them; every body shall look upon them to be like Jericho, an anathema; so that, even when peace returns, they shall not be rebuilt, but shall be thrown to the waste: <hi type="italic">A joy of wild asses and a pasture of flocks.</hi> Thus is many a house brought to ruin by sin. <hi type="italic">Jam seges est ubi Troja fuit—Corn grows on the site of Troy.</hi> <div eID="gen16177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16178" type="x-p"/> 2. In the foresight of this let them <hi type="italic">tremble</hi> and <hi type="italic">be troubled, strip themselves, and gird sackcloth upon their loins,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.32.11">v. 11</reference>. This intimates not only that when the calamity comes they shall thus be made to tremble and be forced to strip themselves, that then God's judgments would strip them and make them bare, but, (1.) That the best prevention of the trouble would be to repent and humble themselves for their sin, and lie in the dust before God in true remorse and godly sorrow, which would be the lengthening out of their tranquillity. This is meeting God in the way of his judgments, and saving a correction by correcting our own mistakes. Those only shall break that will not bend. (2.) That the best preparation for the trouble would be to deny themselves and live a life of mortification, and to sit loose to all the delights of sense. Those that have already by a holy contempt of this world stripped themselves can easily bear to be stripped when trouble and death come. <div eID="gen16178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16179" type="x-p"/> II. While there was still a remnant that kept their integrity they had reason to hope for good times at length and such times the prophet here gives them a pleasant prospect of. Such times they saw in the latter end of the reign of Hezekiah; but the prophecy may well be supposed to look further, to the days of the Messiah, who is <hi type="italic">King of righteousness</hi> and <hi type="italic">King of peace,</hi> and to whom all the prophets bear witness. Now observe, <div eID="gen16179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16180" type="x-p"/> 1. How those blessed times shall be introduced-by the <hi type="italic">pouring out of the Spirit from on high</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.15">v. 15</reference>), which speaks not only of the good-will of God towards us, but the good work of God in us; for then, and not till then, there will be good times, when God by his grace gives men good hearts; and therefore God's <hi type="italic">giving his Holy Spirit to those that ask him</hi> is in effect his giving them all good things, as appears by comparing <reference osisRef="Luke.11.13">Luke xi. 13</reference> with <reference osisRef="Matt.7.11">Matt. vii. 11</reference>. This is the great thing that God's people comfort themselves with the hopes of, that <hi type="italic">the Spirit shall be poured out upon them,</hi> that there shall be a more plentiful effusion of the Spirit of grace than formerly, according as the necessity of the church, in its desolate estate, calls for. This comes from on high, and therefore they look up to their Father in heaven for it. When God designs favours for his church he pours out his Spirit, both to prepare his people to receive his favours and to qualify and give success to those whom he designs to employ as instruments of his favour; for their endeavours to repair the desolations of the church are all fruitless <hi type="italic">until the Spirit be poured out upon them</hi> and then the work is done suddenly. The kingdom of the Messiah was brought in, and set up, by the pouring out of the Spirit (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.1-Acts.2.13">Acts ii.</reference>), and so it is still kept up, and will be to the end. <div eID="gen16180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16181" type="x-p"/> 2. What a wonderfully happy change shall then be made. That which was <hi type="italic">a wilderness,</hi> dry and barren, <hi type="italic">shall become a fruitful field,</hi> and that which we now reckon <hi type="italic">a fruitful field,</hi> in comparison with what it shall be then, <hi type="italic">shall be counted for a forest. Then shall the earth yield her increase.</hi> It is promised that in the days of the Messiah the <hi type="italic">fruit of the earth shall shake like Lebanon,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.72.16">Ps. lxxii. 16</reference>. Some apply this to the admission of the Gentiles into the gospel church (which made the wilderness a fruitful field), and the rejection and exclusion of the Jews, which made that a forest which had been a fruitful field. On the Gentiles was poured out a spirit of life, but on the Jews a spirit of slumber. See what is the evidence and effect of the pouring out of the Spirit upon any soul; it is thereby made fruitful, and has its fruit unto holiness. Three things go to make these times happy:— <div eID="gen16181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16182" type="x-p"/> (1.) Judgment and righteousness, <reference osisRef="Isa.32.16">v. 16</reference>. When the Spirit is poured out upon a land, <hi type="italic">then judgment shall dwell in the wilderness</hi> and turn it into a fruitful field, and <hi type="italic">righteousness shall remain in the fruitful field</hi> and make it yet more fruitful. Ministers shall expound the law and magistrates execute it, and both so judiciously and faithfully that by both the bad shall be made good and the good made better. Among all sorts of people, the poor and low and unlearned, that are neglected as the wilderness, and the rich and great and learned, that are valued as the fruitful field, there shall be right thoughts of things, good principles commanding, and conscience made of good and evil, sin and duty. Or in all parts of the land, both champaign and enclosed, country and city, the ruder parts and those that are more cultivated and refined, justice shall be duly administered. The law of Christ introduces a judgment or rule by which we must be governed, and the gospel of Christ a righteousness by which we must be saved; and, wherever the Spirit is poured out, both these dwell and remain as an everlasting righteousness. <div eID="gen16182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16183" type="x-p"/> (2.) Peace and quietness, <reference osisRef="Isa.32.17-Isa.32.18">v. 17, 18</reference>. The peace here promised is of two kinds:— <div eID="gen16183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16184" type="x-p"/> [1.] Inward peace, <reference osisRef="Isa.32.17">v. 17</reference>. This follows upon the indwelling of righteousness, <reference osisRef="Isa.32.16">v. 16</reference>. Those in whom that work is wrought shall experience this blessed product of it. It is itself peace, and the effect of it is <hi type="italic">quietness and assurance for ever,</hi> that is, a holy serenity and security of mind, by which the soul enjoys itself and enjoys its God, and it is not in the power of this world to disturb it in those enjoyments. Note, Peace, and quietness, and everlasting assurance may be expected, and shall be found, in the way and work of righteousness. True satisfaction is to be had only in true religion, and there it is to be had without fail. Those are the quiet and peaceable lives that are spent <hi type="italic">in all godliness and honesty,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.2">1 Tim. ii. 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Even <hi type="italic">the work of righteousness shall be peace.</hi> In the doing of our duty we shall find abundance of true pleasure, a present great reward of obedience in obedience. Though the work of righteousness may be toilsome and costly, and expose us to contempt, yet it is peace, such peace as is sufficient to bear our charges. <hi type="italic">Secondly, The effect of righteousness shall be quietness and assurance,</hi> not only to the end of time, of our time, and in the end, but to the endless ages of eternity. Real holiness is real happiness now and shall be perfect happiness, that is, perfect holiness, for ever. <div eID="gen16184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16185" type="x-p"/> [2.] Outward peace, <reference osisRef="Isa.32.18">v. 18</reference>. It is a great mercy when those who by the grace of God have quiet and peaceable spirits are by the providence of God made to <hi type="italic">dwell in quiet and peaceable habitations,</hi> not disturbed in their houses or solemn assemblies. When the terror of Sennacherib's invasion was over, the people, no doubt, were more sensible than ever of the mercy of a quiet habitation, not disturbed with the alarms of war. Let every family study to keep itself quiet from strifes and jars within, not two against three and three against two in the house, and then put itself under God's protection to dwell safely, and to be <hi type="italic">quiet from the fear of evil</hi> without. Jerusalem shall be a peaceable habitation; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.33.20">ch. xxxiii. 20</reference>. Even <hi type="italic">when it shall hail,</hi> and there shall be a violent battering storm <hi type="italic">coming down on the forest</hi> that lies bleak, then shall Jerusalem be <hi type="italic">a quiet resting-place, for the city shall be low in a low place,</hi> under the wind, not exposed (as those cities are that stand high) to the fury of the storm, but sheltered by the <hi type="italic">mountains that are round about Jerusalem,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.125.2">Ps. cxxv. 2</reference>. The <hi type="italic">high forts and towers are brought down</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.14">v. 14</reference>), but the city that lies low shall be a quiet resting-place. Those are most safe, and may dwell most at ease, that are humble, and are willing to dwell low, <reference osisRef="Isa.32.19">v. 19</reference>. Those that would dwell in a peaceable habitation must be willing to dwell low, and in a low place. Some think here is an allusion to the preservation of the land of Goshen from the plague of hail, which made great destruction in the land of Egypt. <div eID="gen16185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16186" type="x-p"/> (3.) Plenty and abundance. There shall be such good crops gathered in every where, and every year, that the husbandmen shall be commended, and though happy, who <hi type="italic">sow beside all water</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.20">v. 20</reference>), who sow all the grounds that are fit for seedness, who <hi type="italic">cast their bread,</hi> or bread-corn, <hi type="italic">upon the water,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.1">Eccl. xi. 1</reference>. God will give the increase, but then the husbandman must be industrious, and mind his business, and sow beside all waters; and, if he do this, the corn shall come up so thick and rank that he shall turn in his cattle, even the ox and the ass, to eat the tops of it and keep it under. This is applicable, [1.] To the preaching of the word. Some think it points at the ministry of the apostles, who, as husbandmen, went forth to sow their seed (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.3">Matt. xiii. 3</reference>); they sowed beside all waters; they preached the gospel wherever they came. Waters signify people, and they preached to multitudes. Wherever they found men's hearts softened, and moistened, and disposed to receive the word, they cast in the good seed. And whereas, by the law of Moses, the Jews were forbidden to <hi type="italic">plough with an ox and an ass together</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.22.10">Deut. xxii. 10</reference>), which intimated that Jews and Gentiles should not intermix, now that distinction shall be taken away, and both the ox and the ass, both Jews and Gentiles, shall be employed in, and enjoy the benefit of, the gospel husbandry. [2.] To works of charity. When God sends these happy times blessed are those that improve them in doing good with what they have, that sow beside all waters, that embrace all opportunities of relieving the necessitous; for in due season they shall reap.  <chapter eID="Isa.32"/> <div eID="gen16186" type="x-p"/>

entries.a6dc44b56f15e90d6f77ff039feb6650a6f6e911: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8896"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 32</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.32.1-Isa.32.20">Is 32:1-20</reference>. Messiah's Kingdom; Desolations, to Be Succeeded by Lasting Peace, the Spirit Having Been Poured Out.</title> <div sID="gen14894" type="x-p"/> The times of purity and happiness which shall follow the defeat of the enemies of Jehovah's people (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.1-Isa.32.8">Is 32:1-8</reference>). The period of wrath before that happy state (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.9-Isa.32.14">Is 32:9-14</reference>). The assurance of the final prosperity of the Church is repeated (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.15-Isa.32.20">Is 32:15-20</reference>).<div eID="gen14894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14895" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8896"/><hi type="bold">1. king--</hi>not Hezekiah, who was already on the throne, whereas a future time is contemplated. If he be meant at all, it can only be as a type of Messiah the King, to whom alone the language is fully applicable (<reference osisRef="Hos.3.5">Ho 3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.9.9">Zec 9:9</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="Isa.11.3-Isa.11.5">Is 11:3-5</reference>). The kingdom shall be transferred from the world kings, who have exercised their power against God, instead of for God, to the rightful King of kings (<reference osisRef="Ezek.21.27">Eze 21:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.7.13">Da 7:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.14">14</reference>).<div eID="gen14895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14896" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">princes--</hi>subordinate; referring to all in authority under Christ in the coming kingdom on earth, for example, the apostles, &c. (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.30">Lu 22:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.2">1Co 6:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.12">2Ti 2:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.2.26">Re 2:26</reference>, 27; 3:21). <div eID="gen14896" type="x-p"/>
entries.8e015653dde45561a944ce0f94268e7ce8cc4409: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8897"/><div sID="gen14897" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8897"/><hi type="bold">2. a man--</hi>rather, the man Christ [Lowth]; it is as "the Son of man" He is to reign, as it was as Son of man He suffered (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.64">Mt 26:64</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.5.27">Joh 5:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.19.5">19:5</reference>). Not as Maurer explains, "every one of the princes shall be," &c.<div eID="gen14897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14898" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rivers--</hi>as refreshing as water and the cool shade are to the heated traveller (<reference osisRef="Isa.35.6">Is 35:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.35.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.41.18">41:18</reference>). <div eID="gen14898" type="x-p"/>
entries.579b6e04da64b4a8a162322e9951d5d9d402d202: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8898"/><div sID="gen14899" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8898"/><hi type="bold">3. them that see--</hi>the seers or prophets.<div eID="gen14899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14900" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">them that hear--</hi>the people under instruction (<reference osisRef="Isa.35.5">Is 35:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.35.6">6</reference>). <div eID="gen14900" type="x-p"/>
entries.4d0f42f97e2b7029d646450e208f25bffe264555: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8899"/><div sID="gen14901" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8899"/><hi type="bold">4. rash--</hi>rather, "the hasty"; contrast "shall not make haste" (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.16">Is 28:16</reference>); the reckless who will not take time to weigh religious truth aright. Or else, the well-instructed [Horsley].<div eID="gen14901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14902" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stammers--</hi>those who speak confusedly on divine things (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.4.10-Exod.4.12">Ex 4:10-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.1.6">Jr 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.10.19">Mt 10:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.20">20</reference>). Or, rather, those drunken scorners who in stammering style imitated Isaiah's warnings to mock them [Maurer] (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.7-Isa.11.13">Is 28:7-11, 13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.22">14, 22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.29.20">29:20</reference>); in this view, translate, "speak uprightly" (agreeably to the divine law); not as English Version, referring to the distinctness of articulation, "plainly." <div eID="gen14902" type="x-p"/>
entries.74f0cb4f4e3b4957020886df7fb827a98daf640c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8900"/><div sID="gen14903" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8900"/><hi type="bold">5. vile--</hi>rather, "fool" [Lowth]; that is, ungodly (<reference osisRef="Ps.14.1">Psa 14:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.74.18">74:18</reference>).<div eID="gen14903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14904" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">liberal--</hi>rather, "noble-minded."<div eID="gen14904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14905" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">churl--</hi>rather, "fraudulent" [Gesenius].<div eID="gen14905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14906" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bountiful--</hi>religiously. The atheistic churl, who envies the believer his hope "full of immortality," shall no longer be held as a patriot struggling for the emancipation of mankind from superstition [Horsley]. <div eID="gen14906" type="x-p"/>
entries.f394bd1a02ae3b111583debbd8d437f14d451373: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8901"/><div sID="gen14907" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8901"/><hi type="bold">6. vile ... villainy--</hi>rather, "the (irreligious) fool ... (his) folly."<div eID="gen14907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14908" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">will speak--</hi>rather, "present"; for (so far is the "fool" from deserving the epithet "noble-minded") the fool "speaketh" folly and "worketh," &c.<div eID="gen14908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14909" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hypocrisy--</hi>rather, "profligacy" [Horsley].<div eID="gen14909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14910" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">error--</hi>impiety, perverse arguments.<div eID="gen14910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14911" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hungry--</hi>spiritually (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.6">Mt 5:6</reference>). <div eID="gen14911" type="x-p"/>
entries.040c8df9787907d5353d29bf28c568663e8a5c84: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8902"/><div sID="gen14912" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8902"/><hi type="bold">7. churl--</hi>"the fraudulent"; this verse refers to the last clause of <reference osisRef="Isa.32.5">Is 32:5</reference>; as <reference osisRef="Isa.32.6">Is 32:6</reference> referred to its first clause.<div eID="gen14912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14913" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">speaketh right--</hi>pleadeth a just cause (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.21">Is 29:21</reference>); spiritually, "the poor man's cause" is the divine doctrine, his rule of faith and practice. <div eID="gen14913" type="x-p"/>
entries.fe6f1dae5df14d2f6428cb8cd1e087b451add305: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8903"/><div sID="gen14914" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8903"/><hi type="bold">8. liberal--</hi>rather, "noble-minded."<div eID="gen14914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14915" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stand--</hi>shall be approved under the government of the righteous King. <div eID="gen14915" type="x-p"/>
entries.8d4aeb904b0db673c3760a5d91b2c31866d799bc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8904"/><div sID="gen14916" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8904"/><hi type="bold">9-20. Address to the women of Jerusalem who troubled themselves little about the political signs of the times, but lived a life of self-indulgence (<reference osisRef="Isa.3.16-Isa.3.23">Is 3:16-23</reference>); the failure of food through the devastations of the enemy is here foretold, being what was most likely to affect them as mothers of families, heretofore accustomed to every luxury. Vitringa understands "women--</hi>daughters" as the cities and villages of Judea (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.1-Ezek.16.63">Eze 16:1-63</reference>). See <reference osisRef="Amos.6.1">Am 6:1</reference>. <div eID="gen14916" type="x-p"/>

entries.cd88744b1116f59e48bb9cb906e2160c5eeae6a2: <div eID="gen27795" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen27796" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27797" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27797" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27796" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27798" type="x-p"/> Prophecy of great prosperity under Hezekiah; but, in its highest sense, applicable to Christ, <reference osisRef="Isa.32.1-Isa.32.8">Isa 32:1-8</reference>. Description of impending calamities, <reference osisRef="Isa.32.9-Isa.32.14">Isa 32:9-14</reference>. Rejection of the Jews, and calling of the Gentiles, <reference osisRef="Isa.32.15">Isa 32:15</reference>. The future prosperity of the Church, <reference osisRef="Isa.32.16-Isa.32.20">Isa 32:16-20</reference>. <div eID="gen27798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27799" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen27799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27800" type="x-p"/> Behold, a king shall reign in righteousness - If King Hezekiah were a type of Christ, then this prophecy may refer to his time; but otherwise it seems to have Hezekiah primarily in view. It is evident, however, that in the fullest sense these words cannot be applied to any man; God alone can do all that is promised here. <div eID="gen27800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27801" type="x-p"/> And princes - ושרים ve-sarim, without ל lamed, to; so the ancient Versions. An ancient MS. has ושריו vesaraiv, and his princes.
entries.364e11e5af47598ed60d14d6c6d6ff81a1cb1d3d: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen27801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27802" type="x-p"/> As the shadow of a great rock - The shadow of a great projecting rock is the most refreshing that is possible in a hot country, not only as most perfectly excluding the rays of the sun, but also as having in itself a natural coolness, which it reflects and communicates to every thing about it. <div eID="gen27802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27803" type="x-p"/> Speluncaeque tegant, et saxea procubet umbra. <div eID="gen27803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27804" type="x-p"/> Virg. Georg. 3:145. "Let the cool cave and shady rock protect them." Επει κεφαλην και γουνατα Σειριος αζει, Αυαλεος δε τε χρως απο καυματος· αλλα τοτ' ηδη Ειη πετραιη τε σκιν, και Βιβλινος οινος. <div eID="gen27804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27805" type="x-p"/> Hesiod. 2:206. "When Sirius rages, and thine aching head, <div eID="gen27805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27806" type="x-p"/> Parched skin, and feeble knees refreshment need; <div eID="gen27806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27807" type="x-p"/> Then to the rock's projected shade retire, <div eID="gen27807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27808" type="x-p"/> With Biblin wine recruit thy wasted powers."
entries.24b1c01eaf397f40dba1be39bc27d046808ea5eb: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen27808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27809" type="x-p"/> And the eyes of them that see shall not be dim "And him the eyes of those that see shall regard" - For ולא velo, and not, Le Clerc reads ולו velo, and to him, of which mistake the Masoretes acknowledge there are fifteen instances; and many more are reckoned by others. The removal of the negative restores to the verb its true and usual sense.
entries.c9edfc6ce1184d46905e1a5deaa66fb9c6a6d56f: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen27809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27810" type="x-p"/> The vile person shall no more be called liberal - The different epithets here employed require minute explanation. <div eID="gen27810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27811" type="x-p"/> The vile person - נבל nabal, the pampered, fattened, brainless fellow, who eats to live, and lives to eat; who will scarcely part with any thing, and that which he does give he gives with an evil eye and a grudging heart. <div eID="gen27811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27812" type="x-p"/> Liberal - נדיב nadib; the generous, openhearted, princely man, who writes on all his possessions, For myself and mankind, and lives only to get and to do good. <div eID="gen27812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27813" type="x-p"/> The churl - כילי kilai, the avaricious man; he who starves himself amidst his plenty, and will not take the necessaries of life for fear of lessening his stock. <div eID="gen27813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27814" type="x-p"/> Thus he differs from נבל nabal, who feeds himself to the full, and regards no one else; like the rich man in the Gospel. The avaricious man is called כילי kilai, from כי ki, for, לי li, myself; or contracted from כל col, all, and לי li, to myself: all is mine; all I have is my own; and all I can get is for myself: and yet this man enjoys nothing; he withholds <div eID="gen27814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27815" type="x-p"/> From back and belly too their proper fare: - <div eID="gen27815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27816" type="x-p"/> O cursed lust of gold, when for thy sake <div eID="gen27816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27817" type="x-p"/> The wretch throws up his interest in both worlds, <div eID="gen27817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27818" type="x-p"/> First starved in this, then damned in that to come! <div eID="gen27818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27819" type="x-p"/> Bountiful - שוע shoa, he who is abundantly rich; who rejoices in his plenty, and deals out to the distressed with a liberal hand.
entries.014ee41c724f49d0aa4fd108ab879ced6e139bd1: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen27819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27820" type="x-p"/> The vile person will speak villany "The fool will still utter folly" - A sort of proverbial saying, which Euripides (Bacchae, 369) has expressed in the very same manner and words: Μωρα γαρ μωρος λεγει· "The fool speaks folly. "Of this kind of simple and unadorned proverb or parable, see De S. Poes, Hebr. Praelect. xxiv. <div eID="gen27820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27821" type="x-p"/> Against the Lord "Against Jehovah" - For אל El, two MSS. read אל al, more properly; but both are of nearly the same meaning.
entries.513738f3eae603c3870ed9dd76ba8aaef198f056: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen27821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27822" type="x-p"/> The instruments also of the churl are evil "As for the niggard, his instruments are evil" - His machinations, his designs. The paronomasia, which the prophet frequently deals in, suggested this expression וכלי כליו vechelai kelaiv. The first word is expressed with some variety in the MSS. Seven MSS. read וכילי vekili, one וכל vechol, another וכולי vecoli. <div eID="gen27822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27823" type="x-p"/> To destroy the poor with lying words "To defeat the assertions of the poor in judgment" - A word seems to have been lost here, and two others to have suffered a small alteration, which has made the sentence very obscure. The Septuagint have happily retained the rendering of the lost word, and restored the sentence in all its parts: Και διασκεδασαι λογους ταπεινων εν κρισει· ולהפר דברי אביון במשפט ulehapher dibrey ebyon bemishpat, "And disperse the words of the poor in judgment. "They frequently render the verb הפר haphar by διασκεδασαι, A MS. reads ולדבר uledabber, which gives authority for the preposition ל lamed, to, necessary to the sense, and the Septuagint, Syriac, and Chaldee read במשפט bemishpat, In judgment.
entries.a8e33df24ba179b82a998074914a9d0b331c740e: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen27823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27824" type="x-p"/> Liberal things "Generous purposes" - "Of the four sorts of persons mentioned <reference osisRef="Isa.32.5">Isa 32:5</reference>, three are described, <reference osisRef="Isa.32.6">Isa 32:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.32.7">Isa 32:7</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Isa.32.8">Isa 32:8</reference>, but not the fourth." - Secker. Perhaps for והוא vehu, and he, we ought to read ושוע veshoa, the bountiful.
entries.b4cdbfb2400bbea92b238052fef80881c1c61e10: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen27824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27825" type="x-p"/> Rise up, ye women "ye provinces. "Ye careless daughters "ye cities." - Targum. <div eID="gen27825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27826" type="x-p"/> From this verse to the end of the fourteenth, the desolation of Judea by the Chaldeans appears to be foretold.
entries.76d2693b6858ada3f91a5671285d2f11cc4c0acc: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen27826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27827" type="x-p"/> Gird sackcloth - שק sak, sackcloth, a word necessary to the sense, is here lost, but preserved by the Septuagint, MSS. Alex. and Pachom., and 1. D. II., and edit. Ald. and Comp., and the Arabic and Syriac. <div eID="gen27827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27828" type="x-p"/> Tremble - be troubled - strip you - פשטה peshotah, רגזה regazah, etc. These are infinitives, with a paragogic ה he, according to Schultens, Institut. Ling. Hebr. p. 453, and are to be taken in an imperative sense.
entries.663976db98ad3840d9c2c4954192ef9ffcb9a575: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen27828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27829" type="x-p"/> They shall lament - for the pleasant fields "Mourn ye for the pleasant field" - The Septuagint, Syriac, and Vulgate read ספדו siphdu, mourn ye, imperative; twelve MSS., (five ancient), two editions, the Septuagint, Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, Syriac, and Vulgate, all read שדה sadeh, a field; not שדי shedey, breasts.
entries.fecaaab1dcbd904fee25f473d960898e4dd5c064: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen27829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27830" type="x-p"/> Shall come up thorns and briers "The thorn and the brier shall come up" - All the ancient Versions read ושמיר veshamir, with the conjunction. And an ancient MS. has תעלה בו taaleh bo, "shall come up in it, "which seems to be right; or rather בה bah: and there is a rasure in the place of בו bo in another ancient MS. <div eID="gen27830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27831" type="x-p"/> Yea, upon all the houses of joy - For כי ki, the ancient Versions, except the Vulgate, seem to have read ו ve. כי ki may perhaps be a mistake for בו bo, or בה bah, in it, above mentioned. It is not necessary in this place. <div eID="gen27831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27832" type="x-p"/> The description of impending distress which begins at <reference osisRef="Isa.32.13">Isa 32:13</reference> belongs to other times than that of Sennacherib's invasion, from which they were so soon delivered. It must at least extend to the ruin of the country and city by the Chaldeans. And the promise of blessings which follows was not fulfilled under the Mosaic dispensation; they belong to the Kingdom of Messiah. Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.32.15">Isa 32:15</reference> with <reference osisRef="Isa.29.17">Isa 29:17</reference> (note), and see the note there.
entries.7ceaba3cdb1819946898cddb8fdcdbf77dbacbe8: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen27832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27833" type="x-p"/> The palaces shall be forsaken - The house of the sanctuary (the temple) shall be destroyed. - Targum. <div eID="gen27833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27834" type="x-p"/> The forts "Ophel" - It was a part of Mount Zion, rising higher than the rest, at the eastern extremity, near to the temple, a little to the south of it; called by Micah, <reference osisRef="Mic.4.8">Mic 4:8</reference>, "Ophel of the daughter of Zion. "It was naturally strong by its situation; and had a wall of its own, by which it was separated from the rest of Zion.
entries.f36567fd5fc203f87ff682488f49de3567dd2d0f: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen27834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27835" type="x-p"/> And the fruitful field - והכרמל vehaccarmel. So fifteen MSS., six ancient, and two editions; which seems to make the noun an appellative.
entries.acdd95a390121abf427b87d3993324393759461a: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen27835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27836" type="x-p"/> The work of righteousness - Righteousness works and produces peace. <div eID="gen27836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27837" type="x-p"/> The effect of righteousness - עבדת abodath, the culture. Righteousness, cultivated by peace, produces tranquillity of mind and permanent security. Reader, hast thou the principle? If so, dost thou cultivate it? If thou dost, thou hast peace of conscience, joy in the Holy Ghost, and a sure and certain hope of everlasting life.
entries.78b8630cb98c6dfee23cd624444bc87157f5f80e: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen27837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27838" type="x-p"/> The city shalt be low all a low place. "The city shall be laid level with the plain" - For ובשפלה ubashephelah, the Syriac reads וכשפלה ukeshephelah. The city - probably Nineveh or Babylon: but this verse is very obscure. Saltus; Assyriorum regnum: civitas; magnifica Assyriorum castra. Ephrem Syr. ire loc. For וברד ubarad, a MS. has וירד vaiyered; and so conjectured Abp. Secker, referring to <reference osisRef="Zac.11.2">Zac 11:2</reference>.
entries.58086ea1e5a1998716446e8ed0b4ff5bffc592a7: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen27838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27839" type="x-p"/> That sow beside all waters "Who sow your seed in every well-watered place" - Sir John Chardin's note on this place is: "This exactly answers the manner of planting rice; for they sow it upon the water, and before sowing, while the earth is covered with water, they cause the ground to be trodden by oxen, horses, and asses, who go mid-leg deep; and this is the way of preparing the ground for sowing. As they sow the rice on the water, they transplant it in the water. "Harmer's Observ. vol. 1 p. 280. "Rice is the food of two-thirds of mankind." Dr. Arbuthnot. "It is cultivated in most of the eastern countries." Miller. "It is good for all, and at all times." Sir J. Chardin, ib. "Le ris, qui est leur principal aliment et leur froment (i.e., des Siamois), n'est jamais assez arrose; il croit au milieu de l'eau, et les campagnes ou on le cultive ressemblent plutot a de marets que non pas a des terres qu'on laboure aver la charue. Le ris a bien cette force, que quoy qu'il y ait six ou sept pieds d'eau sur lui, il pousse toujours sa tige au dessus; et le tuyau qui le porte s'eleve et croit a proportion de la hauteur de l'eau qui noye son champ. Voyage de l'Eveque de Beryte, p. 144. Paris, 1666. - L. "Rice, which is the principal grain and aliment of the Siamese, can never be too much watered. It grows in the water, and the fields where it is sown resemble marshes rather than fields cultivated by ploughing. Rice has that property that although it be covered with water six or seven feet deep, yet it raises its stalk above it; and this grows long in proportion to the depth of the water by which the field is inundated."  <chapter eID="Isa.32"/> <div eID="gen27839" type="x-p"/>

entries.a79c8eb7a2cf28281c589d26e1c9b88a72770fa9: <reference osisRef="Isa.32.1-Isa.32.2">Isa 32:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen13206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13207" type="x-p"/> For Judah, sifted, delivered, and purified, there now begins a new ear. Righteous government, as a blessing for the people, is the first beneficent fruit. <hi type="italic">“Behold, the king will reign according to righteousness; and the princes, according to right will they command. And every one will be like a shelter from the wind, and a covert from the storm; like water-brooks in a dry place, like the shadow of a gigantic rock in a languishing land.”</hi> The kingdom of Asshur is for ever destroyed; but the kingdom of Judah rises out of the state of confusion into which it has fallen through its God - forgetting policy and disregard of justice. King and princes now rule according to the standards that have been divinely appointed and revealed. The <hi type="italic">Lamed</hi> in <hi type="italic">ūlesârı̄m</hi> (and the princes) is that of reference (<hi type="italic">quod attinet ad</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.16.3">Psa 16:3</reference> and <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.4">Ecc 9:4</reference>), the exponent of the usual <hi type="italic">casus abs.</hi> (<hi type="italic">Ges</hi>. §146, 2); and the two other <hi type="italic">Lameds</hi> are equivalent to κατά, <hi type="italic">secundum</hi> (as in <reference osisRef="Jer.30.11">Jer 30:11</reference>). The figures in <reference osisRef="Isa.32.2">Isa 32:2</reference> are the same as in Isa 25:4. The rock of Asshur (i.e., Sennacherib) has departed, and the princes of Asshur have deserted their standards, merely to save themselves. The king and princes of Judah are now the defence of their nation, and overshadow it like colossal walls of rock. This is the first fruit of the blessing.
entries.49c781735f1a00c56120b668af23e3c76dea85c6: <reference osisRef="Isa.32.3-Isa.32.4">Isa 32:3-4</reference> <div eID="gen13207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13208" type="x-p"/> The second is an opened understanding, following upon the ban of hardening. <hi type="italic">“And the eyes of the seeing no more are closed, and the ears of the hearing attend. And the heart of the hurried understands to know, and the tongue of stammerers speaks clear things with readiness.”</hi> It is not physical miracles that are predicted here, but a spiritual change. The present judgment of hardening will be repealed: this is what <reference osisRef="Isa.32.3">Isa 32:3</reference> affirms. The spiritual defects, from which many suffer who do not belong to the worst, will be healed: this is the statement in Isa 32:4. The form תּשׁעינה is not the future of שׁעה here, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.31.1">Isa 31:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.22.4">Isa 22:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.17.7-Isa.17.8">Isa 17:7-8</reference> (in the sense of, they will no longer stare about restlessly and without aim), but of שׁעה = שׁעע, a metaplastic future of the latter, in the sense of, to be smeared over to closed (see <reference osisRef="Isa.29.9">Isa 29:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.6.10">Isa 6:10</reference>; cf., <hi type="italic">tach</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.44.18">Isa 44:18</reference>). On <hi type="italic">qâshabh</hi> (the <hi type="italic">kal</hi> of which is only met with here), see at Isa 21:7. The times succeeding the hardening, of which Isaiah is speaking here, are “the last times,” as <reference osisRef="Isa.6.1-Isa.6.13">Isa 6:1-13</reference> clearly shows; though it does not therefore follow that the king mentioned in <reference osisRef="Isa.32.1">Isa 32:1</reference> (as in Isa 11:1.) is the Messiah Himself. In <reference osisRef="Isa.32.1">Isa 32:1</reference> the prophet merely affirms, that Israel as a national commonwealth will then be governed in a manner well pleasing to God; here he predicts that Israel as a national congregation will be delivered from the judgment of not seeing with seeing eyes, and not hearing with hearing ears, and that it will be delivered from defects of weakness also. The <hi type="italic">nimhârı̄m</hi> are those that fall headlong, the precipitate, hurrying, or rash; and the עלּגים, stammerers, are not scoffers (Isa 28:7., <reference osisRef="Isa.19.20">Isa 19:20</reference>), as Knobel and Drechsler maintain, but such as are unable to think and speak with distinctness and certainty, more especially concerning the exalted things of God. The former would now have the gifts of discernment (<hi type="italic">yâbhı̄n</hi>), to perceive things in their true nature, and to distinguish under all circumstances that which is truly profitable (<hi type="italic">lâda‛ath</hi>); the latter would be able to express themselves suitably, with refinement, clearness, and worthiness. <hi type="italic">Tsachōth</hi> (old ed. <hi type="italic">tsâchōth</hi>) signifies that which is light, transparent; not merely intelligible, but refined and elegant. תּמהר gives the adverbial idea to <hi type="italic">ledabbēr</hi> (Ewald, §§285,<hi type="italic">a</hi>).
entries.d5691742404d843d4a4cba753afffa39f380b01f: <reference osisRef="Isa.32.5-Isa.32.8">Isa 32:5-8</reference> <div eID="gen13208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13209" type="x-p"/> A third fruit of the blessing is the naming and treating of every one according to his true character. <hi type="italic">“The fool will no more be called a nobleman, nor the crafty a gentleman. For a fool speaks follies, and his heart does godless things, to practise tricks and to speak error against Jehovah, to leave the soul of hungry men empty, and to withhold the drink of thirsty ones. And the craft of a crafty man is evil, who devises stratagems to destroy suffering ones by lying words, even when the needy exhibits his right. But a noble man devises noble things, and to noble things he adheres.”</hi> Nobility of birth and wealth will give place to nobility of character, so that the former will not exist or not be recognised without the latter. <hi type="italic">Nâdı̄bh</hi> is properly one who is noble in character, and then, dropping the ethical meaning, one who is noble by rank. The meaning of the word <hi type="italic">generosus</hi> follows the same course in the opposite direction. <hi type="italic">Shōă‛</hi> is the man who is raised to eminence by the possession of property; the gentleman, as in Job 34:19. The prophet explains for himself in what sense he uses the words <hi type="italic">nâbhâl</hi> and <hi type="italic">kı̄lai</hi>. We see from his explanation that <hi type="italic">kı̄lai</hi> neither signifies the covetous, from <hi type="italic">kūl</hi> (Saad.), nor the spendthrift, from <hi type="italic">killâh</hi> (Hitzig). Jerome gives the correct rendering, viz., <hi type="italic">fraudulentus</hi>; and Rashi and Kimchi very properly regard it as a contraction of <hi type="italic">nekhı̄lai</hi>. It is an adjective form derived from כּיל = נכיל, like שׂיא = נשׂיא (<reference osisRef="Job.20.6">Job 20:6</reference>). The form כּלי in <reference osisRef="Isa.32.1">Isa 32:1</reference> is used interchangeably with this, merely for the sake of the resemblance in sound to כּליו (machinatoris machinae pravae). In <reference osisRef="Isa.32.6">Isa 32:6</reference>, commencing with <hi type="italic">ki</hi> (for), the fact that the <hi type="italic">nâbhâl</hi> (fool) and <hi type="italic">kı̄lai</hi> (crafty man) will lose their titles of honour, is explained on the simple ground that such men are utterly unworthy of them. <hi type="italic">Nâbhâl</hi> is a scoffer at religion, who thinks himself an enlightened man, and yet at the same time has the basest heart, and is a worthless egotist. The infinitives with <hi type="italic">Lamed</hi> show in what the immorality (<hi type="italic">'âven</hi>) consists, with which his heart is so actively employed. In <reference osisRef="Isa.32.6">Isa 32:6</reference>, <hi type="italic">ūbhedabbēr</hi> (“and if he speak”) is equivalent to, “even in the event of a needy man saying what is right and well founded:” <hi type="italic">Vâv</hi> = <hi type="italic">et</hi> in the sense of <hi type="italic">etiam</hi> ((cf., <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.23">2Sa 1:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.31.12">Psa 31:12</reference>; Hos 8:6; <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.6">Ecc 5:6</reference>); according to Knobel, it is equivalent to <hi type="italic">et quidem</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.2">Ecc 8:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.3.11">Amo 3:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.4.10">Amo 4:10</reference>; whereas Ewald regards it as <hi type="italic">Vav conj.</hi> (§283,<hi type="italic">d</hi>), “and by going to law with the needy,” but את־אביון would be the construction in this case (vid., 2Ki 25:6). According to <reference osisRef="Isa.32.8">Isa 32:8</reference>, not only does the noble man devise what is noble, but as such (הוּא) he adheres to it. We might also adopt this explanation, “It is not upon gold or upon chance that he rises;” but according to the Arabic equivalents, <hi type="italic">qūm</hi> signifies <hi type="italic">persistere</hi> here.
entries.67e0c88c3a3e9d0c867a3afb02122184111f8603: <reference osisRef="Isa.32.9-Isa.32.14">Isa 32:9-14</reference> <div eID="gen13209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13210" type="x-p"/> This short address, although rounded off well, is something more than a fragment complete in itself, like the short parabolic piece in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.23-Isa.28.29">Isa 28:23-29</reference>, which commences in a similar manner. It is the last part of the fourth woe, just as that was the last part of the first. It is a side piece to the threatening prophecy of the time of Uzziah-Jotham (Isa 3:16.), and chastises the frivolous self-security of the women of Jerusalem, just as the former chastises their vain and luxurious love of finery. The prophet has now uttered many a woe upon Jerusalem, which is bringing itself to the verge of destruction; but notwithstanding the fact that women are by nature more delicate, and more easily affected and alarmed, than men, he has made no impression upon the women of Jerusalem, to whom he now foretells a terrible undeceiving of their carnal ease, whilst he holds out before them the ease secured by God, which can only be realized on the ruins of the former. <div eID="gen13210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13211" type="x-p"/> The first part of the address proclaims the annihilation of their false ease. <hi type="italic">“Ye contented women, rise up, hear my voice; ye confident daughters, hearken to my speech! Days to the year: then will ye tremble, confident ones! for it is all over with the vintage, the fruit harvest comes to nought. Tremble, contented ones! Quake, ye confident ones! Strip, make yourselves bare, and gird your loins with sackcloth! They smite upon their breasts for the pleasant fields, for the fruitful vine. On the land of my people there come up weeds, briers; yea, upon all joyous houses of the rejoicing city. For the palace is made solitary; the crowd of the city is left desolate; the ofel and watch-tower serve as caves for ever, for the delight of wild asses, for the tending of flocks.”</hi> The summons is the same as in <reference osisRef="Gen.4.23">Gen 4:23</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.9.19">Jer 9:19</reference> (comp. <reference osisRef="Isa.28.23">Isa 28:23</reference>); the attributes the same as in <reference osisRef="Amos.6.1">Amo 6:1</reference> (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.4.1">Isa 4:1</reference>, where Isaiah apostrophizes the women of Samaria). שׁאנן, lively, of good cheer; and בּטח, trusting, namely to nothing. They are to rise up (<hi type="italic">qōmnâh</hi>), because the word of God must be heard standing (Jdg 3:20). The definition of the time “days for a year” (<hi type="italic">yâmı̄m</hi> <hi type="italic">‛al</hi>-<hi type="italic">shânâh</hi>) appears to indicate the length of time that the desolation would last, as the word <hi type="italic">tirgaznâh</hi> is without any <hi type="italic">Vav</hi> <hi type="italic">apod</hi>. (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.65.24">Isa 65:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.1.16-Job.1.18">Job 1:16-18</reference>); but <reference osisRef="Isa.29.1">Isa 29:1</reference> shows us differently, and the <hi type="italic">Vav</hi> is omitted, just as it is, for example, in Dan 4:28. <hi type="italic">Shânâh</hi> is the current year. In an undefined number of days, at the most a year from the present time (which is sometimes the meaning of <hi type="italic">yâmı̄m</hi>), the trembling would begin, and there would be neither grapes nor fruit to gather. Hence the spring harvest of corn is supposed to be over when the devastation begins. ימים is an <hi type="italic">acc. temporis</hi>; it stands here (as in <reference osisRef="Isa.27.6">Isa 27:6</reference>, for example; vid., Ewald, §293, 1) to indicate the starting point, not the period of duration. The <hi type="italic">milel</hi>-forms פּשׁטה, ערה, חגרה ,ערה , are explained by Ewald, Drechsler, and Luzzatto, as <hi type="italic">plur. fem. imper.</hi> with the <hi type="italic">Nun</hi> of the termination <hi type="italic">nâh</hi> dropped - an elision that is certainly never heard of. Others regard it as <hi type="italic">inf.</hi> with <hi type="italic">He femin.</hi> (Credner, <hi type="italic">Joel</hi>, p. 151); but קטלה for the infinitive קטלה is unexampled; and equally unexampled would be the inf. with He indicating the summons, as suggested by Böttcher, “to the shaking!” “to the stripping!” They are <hi type="italic">sing. masc. imper.</hi>, such as occur elsewhere apart from the pause, e.g., מלוכה (for which the <hi type="italic">keri</hi> has מלכה) in Jdg 9:8; and the singular in the place of the plural is the strongest form of command. The masculine instead of the feminine appears already in הרדוּ, which is used in the place of חרדנה. The prophet then proceeds in the singular number, comprehending the women as a mass, and using the most massive expression. The <hi type="italic">He</hi> introduced into the summons required that the feminine forms, רגזי, etc., should be given up. ערה, from ערר, to be naked, to strip one’s self. חגרה absolute, as in <reference osisRef="Joel.1.13">Joe 1:13</reference> (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.3.24">Isa 3:24</reference>), signifies to gird one’s self with sackcloth (<hi type="italic">saq</hi>). We meet with the same remarkable <hi type="italic">enall. generis</hi> in Isa 32:12. Men have no breasts (<hi type="italic">shâdaim</hi>), and yet the masculine <hi type="italic">sōphedı̄m</hi> is employed, inasmuch as the prophet had the whole nation in his mind, throughout which there would be such a <hi type="italic">plangere ubera</hi> on account of the utter destruction of the hopeful harvest of corn and wine. <hi type="italic">Shâdaim</hi> (breasts) and שׂדי (construct to <hi type="italic">sâdōth</hi>) have the same common ring as <hi type="italic">ubera</hi> and <hi type="italic">ubertas frugum</hi>. In <reference osisRef="Isa.32.13">Isa 32:13</reference> <hi type="italic">ta‛ăleh</hi> points back to <hi type="italic">qōts</hi> <hi type="italic">shâmı̄r</hi>, which is condensed into one neuter idea. The <hi type="italic">ki</hi> in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.32.13">Isa 32:13</reference></hi> has the sense of the Latin <hi type="italic">imo</hi> (Ewald, §330,<hi type="italic">b</hi>). The genitive connection of עלּיזה קריה with משׂושׂ בּתּי (joy-houses of the jubilant city) is the same as in Isa 28:1. The whole is grammatically strange, just as in the Psalms the language becomes all the more complicated, disjointed, and difficult, the greater the wrath and indignation of the poet. Hence the short shrill sentences in <reference osisRef="Isa.32.14">Isa 32:14</reference> : palace given up (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.13.22">Isa 13:22</reference>); city bustle forsaken (i.e., the city generally so full of bustle, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.2">Isa 22:2</reference>). The use of בּעד is the same as in <reference osisRef="Prov.6.26">Pro 6:26</reference>; Job 2:4. <hi type="italic">‛Ofel</hi>, i.e., the south-eastern fortified slope of the temple mountain, and the <hi type="italic">bachan</hi> (i.e., the watch-tower, possibly the flock-tower which is mentioned in Mic 4:8 along with <hi type="italic">‛ofel</hi>), would be <hi type="italic">pro speluncis</hi>, i.e., would be considered and serve as such. And in the very place where the women of Jerusalem had once led their life of gaiety, wild asses would now have their delight, and flocks their pasture (on the wild asses, <hi type="italic">perâ'ı̄m</hi>, that fine animal of the woodless steppe, see at <reference osisRef="Job.24.5">Job 24:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.39.5-Job.39.8">Job 39:5-8</reference>). Thus would Jerusalem, with its strongest, proudest places, be laid in ruins, and that in a single year, or ever less than a year.
entries.e5579fe3a914719b75f711b890a9127f24925007: <reference osisRef="Isa.32.15-Isa.32.19">Isa 32:15-19</reference> <div eID="gen13211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13212" type="x-p"/> The state would then continue long, very long, until at last the destruction of the false rest would be followed by the realization of the true. <hi type="italic">“Until the Spirit is poured out over us from on high, and the wilderness becomes a fruitful field, and the fruitful field is counted as the forest. And justice makes its abode in the desert, and righteousness settles down upon the fruit-field. And the effect of righteousness will be peace, and the reward of righteousness rest and security for ever. And my people dwells in a place of peace, and in trustworthy, safe dwellings, and in cheerful resting-places. And it hails with the overthrow of the forest, and into lowliness must the city be brought low.”</hi> There is a limit, therefore, to the “for ever” of Isa 32:14. The punishment would last till the Spirit, which Israel had not then dwelling in the midst of it (see Hag 2:5), and whose fulness was like a closed vessel to Israel, should be emptied out over Israel from the height of heaven (compare the <hi type="italic">piel</hi> ערה, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.20">Gen 24:20</reference>), i.e., should be poured out in all its fulness. When that was done, a great change would take place, the spiritual nature of which is figuratively represented in the same proverbial manner as in Isa 29:17. At the same time, a different turn is given to the second half in the passage before us. The meaning is, not that what was now valued as a fruit-bearing garden would be brought down from its false eminence, and be only regarded as forest; but that the whole would be so glorious, that what was now valued as a fruit-garden, would be thrown into the shade by something far more glorious still, in comparison with which it would have the appearance of a forest, in which everything grew wild.
